courses.title: Biopharmaceutics and Clinical Pharmacokinetics
courses.description: Drug release and absorption, bioavailability and bioequivalence, compartmental pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, therapeutic drug monitoring and modified-release systems.

topics.title: Biopharmaceutics: From Dosage Form to Absorption
topics.summary: LADME, factors affecting absorption, BCS and food effects.

material.heading: LADME
material.body: Biopharmaceutics links a dosage form's physicochemical properties and formulation to the rate and extent of drug absorption. The LADME scheme: Liberation (release from the dosage form — disintegration and dissolution), Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion. For poorly soluble drugs, dissolution is rate-limiting; for highly soluble drugs, gastric emptying or permeability may limit absorption. Physiological factors: gastrointestinal pH, gastric emptying (slowed by food, anticholinergics, opioids), intestinal transit, surface area, efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein), gut wall and first-pass hepatic metabolism, and disease (diarrhoea, achlorhydria).
keyPoints: Dissolution rate-limiting for poorly soluble drugs

material.heading: BCS and food effects
material.body: The Biopharmaceutics Classification System (Amidon, 1995) groups drugs by solubility and intestinal permeability: Class I (high/high — e.g. metoprolol, paracetamol), Class II (low solubility/high permeability — e.g. ibuprofen, carbamazepine; dissolution-limited, formulation matters), Class III (high solubility/low permeability — e.g. atenolol, metformin), Class IV (low/low — e.g. furosemide in some classifications). BCS-based biowaivers allow waiver of in vivo bioequivalence studies for some Class I (and III) drugs with rapid dissolution. Food effects: food increases absorption of lipophilic drugs (lumefantrine, griseofulvin, albendazole in tissue infections) but reduces absorption of others (e.g. some penicillins, rifampicin, levothyroxine best on an empty stomach); calcium, iron and antacids chelate tetracyclines and quinolones.
keyPoints: Biowaivers for rapidly dissolving Class I drugs
Levothyroxine and rifampicin on empty stomach

topics.title: Bioavailability and Bioequivalence
topics.summary: Absolute and relative bioavailability, Cmax, Tmax and AUC, and bioequivalence criteria.

material.heading: Parameters
material.body: Bioavailability describes the rate and extent to which the active ingredient reaches the systemic circulation. Plasma concentration–time curves give: Cmax (peak concentration — relates to efficacy and toxicity), Tmax (time to peak — rate of absorption) and AUC (area under the curve — extent of absorption, total exposure). Absolute bioavailability F = (AUCoral × DoseIV)/(AUCIV × Doseoral); relative bioavailability compares two non-intravenous formulations. The minimum effective concentration (MEC) and minimum toxic concentration (MTC) define the therapeutic window; onset of action is when levels exceed the MEC and duration is the time above it.

material.heading: Bioequivalence
material.body: Two pharmaceutically equivalent products are bioequivalent if their rate and extent of absorption are similar enough that their efficacy and safety are expected to be the same. Standard criterion: the 90% confidence intervals for the ratios (test/reference) of AUC and Cmax must lie within 80.00–125.00% (narrower for narrow therapeutic index drugs). Studies are usually randomised crossover designs in healthy volunteers with adequate washout (at least 5 half-lives). Generic medicines must demonstrate bioequivalence to the innovator for registration (NAFDAC and WHO prequalification). Therapeutic equivalence allows interchangeable generic substitution, reducing costs.
keyPoints: 90% CI of AUC and Cmax ratios within 80–125%

topics.title: Compartmental Pharmacokinetics
topics.summary: One-compartment models, elimination rate constant, IV bolus and infusion, and oral absorption kinetics.

material.heading: One-compartment model
material.body: In a one-compartment model with first-order elimination after an IV bolus, C = C0e^(−kt), where k (elimination rate constant) = CL/Vd and t½ = 0.693/k. Plotting ln C against time gives a straight line with slope −k. Vd = Dose/C0. Clearance CL = k × Vd = Dose/AUC. For a constant-rate IV infusion, the steady-state concentration Css = infusion rate/CL, reached after about 4–5 half-lives regardless of the rate. A two-compartment model shows an initial distribution (α) phase followed by an elimination (β) phase.

material.heading: Oral absorption and multiple dosing
material.body: After oral dosing, absorption usually follows first-order kinetics with absorption rate constant ka; if ka ≫ k, the terminal slope reflects elimination; if absorption is slower than elimination ('flip-flop' kinetics, e.g. some modified-release products), the terminal slope reflects absorption. With repeated doses at interval τ, drug accumulates until steady state; the accumulation factor = 1/(1 − e^(−kτ)). Average steady-state concentration Css,avg = F × Dose/(CL × τ). Loading dose = Vd × target C/F; maintenance dose rate = CL × target C/F. Fluctuation between peak and trough decreases with shorter intervals or modified-release formulations.
keyPoints: Loading = Vd × C/F; maintenance = CL × C/F

topics.title: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring and Dose Individualisation
topics.summary: Drugs requiring TDM, sampling times, dosing in renal and hepatic impairment, and special populations.

material.heading: TDM
material.body: Therapeutic drug monitoring measures plasma concentrations to optimise dosing for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, large inter-individual variability, a good concentration–response relationship and no easy clinical endpoint: aminoglycosides (gentamicin — trough to avoid toxicity, peak or AUC for efficacy), vancomycin (trough or AUC), digoxin (sample at least 6 hours after the dose; range ~0.5–2 µg/L lower targets now preferred), lithium (12 hours post-dose; 0.4–1.0 mmol/L), phenytoin (zero-order kinetics — small dose changes cause large level changes; correct for low albumin), carbamazepine, theophylline, ciclosporin and tacrolimus. Levels are interpreted with timing of the sample, dosing history, adherence, clinical state and interacting drugs.
keyPoints: TDM for narrow therapeutic index drugs

material.heading: Special populations
material.body: Renal impairment: estimate renal function (Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance = [(140 − age) × weight (kg)] ÷ [0.815 × serum creatinine (µmol/L)] × 0.85 for women); reduce dose or extend interval for renally excreted drugs (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, metformin, dabigatran, many antibiotics), and avoid nephrotoxins. Hepatic impairment: reduce doses of highly metabolised drugs; avoid drugs that precipitate encephalopathy (sedatives, opioids) or bleeding. Children: doses by weight or body surface area; neonates have immature metabolism and renal function (e.g. chloramphenicol — grey baby syndrome). Elderly: reduced renal function and altered body composition; start low, go slow; beware polypharmacy and falls (Beers criteria). Pregnancy: increased Vd and renal clearance; consider teratogenicity. Obesity: use appropriate weight (ideal, adjusted or total) depending on drug lipophilicity.
keyPoints: Elderly: start low, go slow; Beers criteria

topics.title: Modified-release and Novel Drug Delivery Systems
topics.summary: Sustained and controlled release, targeted delivery, transdermal, and nanotechnology.

material.heading: Modified release
material.body: Modified-release (MR) formulations alter the timing or location of drug release: delayed release (enteric coating — releases in the intestine), extended/sustained release (release over an extended period to reduce dosing frequency and fluctuation — e.g. nifedipine MR, metformin XR, carbamazepine CR), and pulsatile release. Mechanisms: matrix systems (hydrophilic hydroxypropyl methylcellulose matrices that swell and gel; inert matrices), reservoir (membrane-controlled) systems, osmotic pumps (OROS — release through a laser-drilled hole at a constant, zero-order rate) and ion-exchange resins. MR tablets must not be crushed or chewed (risk of 'dose dumping' and toxicity); alcohol can cause dose dumping from some formulations. Long-acting injectables include depot antipsychotics, medroxyprogesterone acetate (every 3 months) and benzathine penicillin.

material.heading: Novel systems
material.body: Transdermal patches (nicotine, fentanyl, glyceryl trinitrate, hormonal contraceptives) deliver drugs through the skin for systemic effects, avoiding first-pass metabolism and giving steady levels; heat and broken skin increase absorption. Implants (contraceptive implants such as Jadelle and Implanon; drug-eluting stents) provide long-term release. Inhaled delivery (metered-dose and dry powder inhalers, nebulisers) targets the lungs. Nanotechnology-based systems — liposomes (liposomal amphotericin B, liposomal doxorubicin — reduced toxicity), polymeric nanoparticles, and lipid nanoparticles (mRNA vaccines) — improve solubility, stability and targeting. Antibody–drug conjugates target cancer cells. Such technologies can improve adherence (e.g. long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention).
